aiExplanation: This solution scans every cell of the matrix once, adding the **absolute value** of each number to `sum` (as if every value could be flipped to positive), while counting how many values are negative or zero in `neg` and tracking the **largest non-positive value** (the one closest to zero) in `min` using `Math.max`. Since flips always affect pairs of adjacent numbers, an **even** count of negatives can be fully cancelled out — but if `neg % 2` is odd, one value must stay negative, so the code applies the correction `sum += min - Math.abs(min)`, which subtracts twice the magnitude of that leftover value. The flaw is that `min` only considers non-positive entries, so when the cheapest value to sacrifice is actually a **small positive number**, the correction subtracts more than necessary.

author: Vitor
aiExplanation: This solution relies on the insight that flipping the signs of adjacent pairs lets you cancel out negatives **two at a time**, so the best possible answer is usually the sum of every value's absolute value. It walks the whole matrix once, accumulating `Math.abs(matrix[i][j])` into `sum`, counting non-positive entries in `neg`, and tracking the **smallest absolute value** anywhere in the matrix in `min`. If the count of negatives is even, they can all be flipped to positive and `sum` is returned as-is; if `neg % 2` is odd, exactly one value must remain negative, so it sacrifices the cheapest one by subtracting `2 * min` (its contribution flips from `+min` to `-min`). This runs in **O(m × n)** time with constant extra space.

aiExplanation: This is a cleaned-up version of the same greedy idea: because sign flips happen in **pairs**, any even number of negatives can be eliminated entirely, making the theoretical maximum the sum of all **absolute values**. The code traverses the matrix once, adding each cell's absolute value to `sum`, counting strictly negative cells (`matrix[row][col] < 0`) in `neg`, and remembering the **smallest absolute value** seen in `min`. Note that zeros are deliberately not counted as negatives here — a zero can absorb a leftover flip for free, and since its absolute value is `0` it would drive `min` down anyway. When the negative count is odd, one value is doomed to stay negative, so the code picks the smallest-magnitude one and subtracts `2 * min` from the total. The result is an **O(m × n)** single-pass solution with constant memory.

author: Vitor
aiExplanation: This solution takes a **sort-and-pair** approach instead of the usual counting trick. It first flattens the 2D matrix into a single array using nested `reduce` calls (the inner `reduce` is really just being used to push every element into `acc`), then sorts the values in ascending order so the most negative numbers sit next to each other. It then walks the sorted array **two elements at a time**, summing each pair: if the pair's sum is negative, both members must be negative, so it flips the pair's sign (mimicking the allowed operation of negating two adjacent values) and adds the positive result; otherwise it adds the pair as-is. The `arr[i + 1] || 0` guard handles an odd-length array, where the final "pair" has only one element. Sorting makes this **O(m·n log(m·n))** — slower than the single-pass approach, but it works because pairing negatives after sorting cancels them optimally.

author: Vitor
aiExplanation: This attempt flattens the matrix into `arr` with plain nested loops, sorts it ascending, and then processes the sorted values in **pairs of two**: it computes each pair's sum via `arr[i] + (arr[i + 1] || 0)`, flips the sign if the sum is negative (simulating the operation of negating two values together), and accumulates the result into `total`. The subtle bug lies in the `|| 0` fallback: when `arr[i + 1]` is literally `0`, the expression `0 || 0` still yields `0`, but more importantly a **negative number paired with a zero** produces a negative pair sum that gets flipped to positive — effectively negating a single value for free, which the problem's pairwise-flip rule doesn't always allow. Taking the absolute value of a pair like `[-5, 3]` also credits `2` instead of the correct `-2`, since flipping both would give `5 - 3 = 2` only by spending a flip that may not be free. These edge cases cause wrong answers on certain inputs, hence the **FAILED** status.

author: Vitor
aiExplanation: This version starts from the **plain sum** of every matrix value (accumulated in `total` while flattening the matrix into `arr`), then figures out how much that sum improves by flipping pairs of negatives. After sorting `arr` ascending, the most negative numbers are adjacent, so it walks the array in **consecutive pairs** (`arr[i - 1]` and `arr[i]`): whenever a pair's sum is negative, flipping both values changes the total by exactly `-sum * 2` — the pair's contribution goes from `sum` to `-sum` — so that delta is added to `total`. Pairs whose sum is already non-negative are left alone, since flipping them would only hurt. Iterating from `i = 1` in steps of two also neatly skips any unpaired final element in an odd-length array. The cost is dominated by the sort, giving **O(m·n log(m·n))** time.

aiExplanation: This attempt returns to the single-pass counting strategy: it sweeps the matrix once, adding each value's magnitude to `total` (positives directly, non-positives via `-matrix[r][c]`), counting non-positive entries in `negativeCounter`, and tracking the non-positive value **closest to zero** in `highestNegative` (via `Math.max`, since for example `-2 > -7`). If the bitwise check `negativeCounter & 1` shows an odd count, one value must stay negative, so it adds `highestNegative * 2` — because `highestNegative` is negative, this subtracts twice its magnitude from the total. The bug is the same one from the first attempt: the sacrificed value should be the **smallest absolute value in the entire matrix**, positives included. When a positive number like `1` is smaller in magnitude than every negative, this code overpays, producing a wrong (too small) answer and the **FAILED** status.

author: Vitor
aiExplanation: This final version fixes the earlier mistake by tracking the right value to sacrifice. In a single **O(m × n)** pass it adds every cell's magnitude to `total` (treating each value as if it could be made positive), counts non-positive entries in `negativeCounter`, and — crucially — records the **smallest absolute value across the whole matrix** in `smallestNumber`, checking `Math.abs(matrix[r][c])` for *every* cell rather than only the negative ones. Because the allowed operation flips two adjacent values at once, an even number of negatives can always be cancelled completely; if the bitwise test `negativeCounter & 1` reveals an odd count, exactly one value must end up negative, and the cheapest choice is the one with the smallest magnitude, so `smallestNumber * 2` is subtracted (its contribution swings from positive to negative). This greedy approach solves the problem in one pass with constant extra space.
